source.title: On the Limits of LLM Reasoning: Evidence From Contamination, Translation, and Answer Modification in Multiple-Choice Benchmarks
source.authors: Eva Sánchez-Salido; Julio Gonzalo; G. Marco

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; some appendix tables are flattened, but the main results relevant here are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling laws and relates model size to robustness on modified multiple-choice questions, but it does not measure pretraining cross-entropy, fit or test scaling curves, compare compute-optimal allocations, or test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on model accuracy and its drop after replacing the correct option with “None of the other answers.” Those concern robustness to answer modification, not the loss, scaling curves, or compute allocation named in the versions. The discussion of scaling laws and model size is included as context; no cited scaling-law results are treated as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates 16 off-the-shelf instruction-tuned models on multiple-choice accuracy and on the drop under a 'None of the other answers' (NOTO) substitution. It cites scaling laws (Kaplan et al.) as a contrast, but measures no pretraining loss, fits no curves and runs no controlled scale sweep. Its size comparison concerns a robustness drop across models of different eras, families and training recipes. That is a related but different construct from V6's downstream performance vs scale or loss, so it is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that NOTO exposes large, model-dependent drops: on average 57% on MMLU and 50% on UNED-Access 2024. They read the larger drops on public and original-language data as signs of contamination and memorisation. They also conclude that robustness is not strictly correlated with model size and credit architecture and training strategies (reasoning models) over sheer scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates instruction-following models on multiple-choice accuracy and a NOTO answer-modification variation; it does not fit language-model loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: NOTO accuracy drops vary across models and datasets; the reported association between original accuracy and drop also differs across the four dataset-language conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 16 heterogeneous instruction-tuned models, NOTO accuracy drop does not track size bins (<10B, 10-100B, >100B). The smallest drop is for the medium-sized DeepSeek-R1-70B, and some large models drop steeply. Newer models tend to drop less.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to replacing the correct option with 'None of the other answers' is not predicted by parameter count across model families; release date and training method matter more.

fits_no_version.finding: Base accuracy correlates inversely with NOTO drop (Pearson r from -0.47 to -0.78). The English MMLU correlation is not significant (p=0.067).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard benchmark accuracy only partly predicts a model's robustness to answer-option modification.

record.problems: The paper evaluates only multiple-choice benchmarks, MMLU and UNED-Access 2024, and uses a zero-shot setup; it does not evaluate broader real-world tasks. The model-size robustness comparison is not a controlled scaling sweep, and Figure 2’s size-group results are described without numerical group means.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for original and NOTO accuracy by model, language, and dataset are included: those results measure answer-modification robustness rather than any listed scaling-law version. Model-level table entries are also not needed for the aggregate size/robustness finding recorded in R5.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured.
No fitted laws and no extrapolation.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are scaled.
No controlled relation of downstream scores to scale or pretraining loss. Base accuracy by model is reported but never analysed against size.

record.verdict_notes: The setup text says 15 models, but Table 1 lists 16. The scaling-law mention is rhetorical. The comparison is across uncontrolled model families, several with undisclosed sizes, so it cannot bear on V6 as stated.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as compute varies.
Effect of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; the paper does not test downstream scores against scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices.
